newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway says Arabs should pay more to Palestinians.
newsitem.headline: Norway says Arabs should pay more to Palestinians.

text.p: Norway urged petroleum-wealthy Arab countries on Tuesday to contribute more money to Palestinian aid projects facing financial collapse.

Deputy Foreign Minister Jan Egeland said Arab states gave less than one percent of the general budget of the United Nations Reliefs and Works Agency (UNRWA), which provides international relief to Palestinian refugees.

"Norway calls upon oil-rich Arab countries to respond to the acute economic crisis in the assistance work for the Palestinians," Egeland told Reuters after talks with UNRWA Commissioner General Peter Hansen.

"We criticise the imbalance in the burden-sharing within the donor community. Some of the nations that should be closest to the Palestinian cause are the worst-performing donor countries," Egeland said.

Norway, producing around 3.2 million barrels a day of oil and the second largest crude exporter after Saudi Arabia, will donate 400 million Norwegian crowns ($61.82 million), more than $15 per capita, in aid to Palestinians in 1996. More than a quarter of the total amount will be channelled to UNRWA projects.

The Scandinavian country played a lead role in brokering secret negotiations that led to the signing of the historic peace pact between Israel and the Palestinian Liberation Organisation in 1993. Norway also chairs the Ad-hoc Liaison Committee of countries donating to Palestinian finances.

UNRWA's Hansen told Reuters the agency had cash in hand for eight days of services to the growing Palestinian population. Outstanding pledges would probably cover operations at a reduced level for the rest of the year, but an additional $50 to $70 million would be required in 1997 to get back to the same level of assistance as in 1994, he said.
"We do not know as of now if we can meet the payroll for October. It's a case of staggering from week to week," Hansen said.

UNRWA, which has an annual budget of $400 million, provides education, primary health care and anti-poverty measures such as food distribution to Palestinian refugees. Founded in 1948, it is the largest U.N. agency in terms of manpower with 22,000 staff, including teachers, doctors and nurses.

"Cutting vital services to these refugees who have nothing else will send a terrible message that the world is forgetting them at this stage in the peace process. It will do nothing for stability in the region," the UNRWA commissioner general said.
"It is very important now to reinforce expectations that things are going to get better in the future as a prerequisite for peace."
